Dress and morality : The politics of what women wear
2026-09-07T00:09:01+06:00 | Syeda Shagufe Hossain
https://www.thedailystar.net/slow-reads/wisdom/news/dress-and-morality-the-politics-what-women-wear-4266346

In the early nineteenth century, in the princely state of Travancore, a woman’s covered chest was not simply a matter of personal choice. Arguably, it still isn’t. But there, covering one’s chest could amount to a violation of the caste order. Nadar women, members of a community historically associated with palmyra climbing and toddy tapping, occupied a low position within the caste hierarchy and were prohibited from wearing an upper cloth in the manner permitted to higher-caste women. An uncovered chest was therefore not simply the absence of modesty. It helped make social rank visible.

When Nadar women, some of them newly converted to Christianity and supported by Protestant missionaries, began challenging these restrictions, the response was violent. Women were harassed and stripped; homes, schools and churches were attacked during periods of conflict. In 1859, after decades of struggle, a royal proclamation permitted Nadar women to cover their upper bodies. But the concession did not establish complete sartorial equality: it continued to prohibit them from imitating the styles of higher-caste women. Even in conceding the cloth, authority retained the power to prescribe its form.

A body is assigned a meaning before it has any say in the matter. Adults begin assigning meaning to bodies through categories of sex, caste, race, beauty and belonging long before children understand those categories. At some point, watching becomes internal, and supervision starts to feel like instinct rather than instruction.

A body is assigned a meaning before it has any say in the matter. Adults begin assigning meaning to bodies through categories of sex, caste, race, beauty and belonging long before children understand those categories. At some point, watching becomes internal, and supervision starts to feel like instinct rather than instruction.

Covering: Proof of civilisation

Half a world away, in the same century, Christian missionaries arrived at the opposite conclusion. Dress practices differed across the Pacific, but in several island societies, women’s exposed chests had not carried the sexual and moral meanings that European Christians attributed to them. Missionaries treated bareness as evidence of heathenism and promoted high-necked, long-sleeved dresses derived from European forms as signs of conversion and civilisation. These garments acquired distinct local forms and names, including the holokū and, later, the muʻumuʻu in Hawaiʻi and the tibuta in Kiribati. Pacific women did not merely submit to the new dress: they altered it to suit the climate, movement, ceremony and ideals of beauty, eventually making some of these forms expressions of local identity.

Where caste authority in Travancore restricted covering in order to preserve hierarchy, Pacific missions used covering to demonstrate salvation. The garments were not the same, nor were these chapters part of one continuous history. However, the political operation was common to both. In Travancore, the bare chest was made into visible evidence of inferior status; covering it could constitute an act of insubordination. In missionary encounters across the Pacific, the bare chest was recast as evidence of savagery; covering it became proof of reform. Neither authority discovered the moral meaning of the body. Each assigned one to it. The chest, covered or uncovered, became a surface on which someone else’s social order was written.

Lives of divorced single mothers: What choice costs in a judgmental society

From the andarmahal to the colonial public sphere

Closer to home, nineteenth-century Bengali sari practices did not always resemble the blouse-and-petticoat ensemble now imagined as timelessly traditional. Historian Sonia Nishat Amin describes women inside the Hindu andarmahal , the secluded women’s quarters, wearing light saris without stitched undergarments. This was not necessarily experienced as incomplete dress. It belonged to a domestic world structured by seclusion; when women from elite households began entering colonial public spaces, their clothing became subject to a different visual standard.

In the 1860s, Jnanadanandini Devi, who was married to Satyendranath Tagore, the first Indian to enter the Indian Civil Service, encountered different ways of wearing the sari while living in Bombay. Drawing on Parsi and Gujarati styles, she helped popularise in Bengal an ensemble that paired the sari with a blouse and petticoat and rearranged its pleats and pallu for greater mobility.

The orna a girl is told to adjust today did not always carry the specific instruction now attached to her developing chest. It belongs to a long and changing history of draped upper cloth, but Travancore’s caste regulations, Pacific missionary dress and colonial Bengali respectability are not its successive stages.

The orna a girl is told to adjust today did not always carry the specific instruction now attached to her developing chest. It belongs to a long and changing history of draped upper cloth, but Travancore’s caste regulations, Pacific missionary dress and colonial Bengali respectability are not its successive stages.

A frequently repeated story claims that she was refused entry to a British club because her Bengali sari exposed too much of her torso, but the anecdote is difficult to substantiate and should not be used to explain the entire transformation. The broader pressure is clearer: women entering colonial public and elite social spaces were increasingly required to make their bodies legible according to new standards of respectable dress.

An adaptation turned into tradition

Jnanadanandini’s response was neither simple surrender nor uncomplicated liberation. She adapted rather than discarded the sari, creating an ensemble that enabled movement beyond the household. What began within elite reformist circles spread so widely that later generations could mistake a modern arrangement for an ancient rule. Authority disappeared into tradition. The solution survived the conditions that produced it. But repetition erased the moment of negotiation. Eventually, garments shaped by particular historical pressures no longer appeared to answer caste hierarchy, missionary doctrine or colonial respectability. They simply appeared traditional.

The body as a text

A body, before anyone has spoken to it, carries no instructions. An infant's chest is skin and breath and nothing else. There is no shame in it, no modesty owed to it, and no one yet watching to decide what it means. That condition, however, does not last. Somewhere between infancy and adulthood , a body stops being simply a body and becomes a text: something other people feel entitled to read, and something a girl learns, slowly, to read the way they do, from the outside, as if she were the stranger looking in. Frantz Fanon, writing of a different but related inheritance, put the mechanism in five words: “I am overdetermined from without.”

A body is assigned a meaning before it has any say in the matter. Adults begin assigning meaning to bodies through categories of sex, caste, race, beauty and belonging long before children understand those categories. At some point, watching becomes internal, and supervision starts to feel like instinct rather than instruction. The chest is where this lesson has been taught most often and most inconsistently—a lesson that travels across time and geographies.

The moral hierarchy of blood

Long trail of upper cloth

None of these histories invented the practice of draping cloth around the upper body. In fact, in South Asia, that practice reaches much further back, although the surviving evidence does not permit a neat origin story for the modern orna. Ancient texts and art depict several forms of unstitched upper cloth, often discussed under the term uttariya . Early textiles have not survived; terminology and dress changed across regions and centuries; and a sculpture can show how cloth appears to fall without telling us what its wearer called it or what moral meanings it carried.

What the record does suggest is that draped upper cloth was not always an exclusively female garment with one fixed modesty function. Men and women both wore forms of it, arranged over the shoulder, arms, torso or head for practical, ornamental, ceremonial and status-related purposes. Later representations and prescriptions connected women’s upper cloth with covering the breasts and, in some contexts, the head. A broadly shared practice of draping thus acquired an increasingly unequal moral burden: the arrangement of a woman’s cloth became evidence of sexual respectability and proper conduct in ways that men’s did not.

The evidence of moral character

It would be too simple to draw an unbroken line from the Vedic uttariya through the odhni and dupatta to the Bengali orna. Languages, empires, migrations, religious cultures and regional fashions intervened, and the garments themselves changed. So that is not the claim I am making. I am asking a different question instead—perhaps an unoriginal one, but one that makes the history of this garment heavier: When does fabric become evidence of moral character?

The orna a girl is told to adjust today did not always carry the specific instruction now attached to her developing chest . It belongs to a long and changing history of draped upper cloth, but Travancore’s caste regulations, Pacific missionary dress and colonial Bengali respectability are not its successive stages. They reveal instead how different authorities repeatedly assigned moral and political meanings to clothing: caste hierarchy could make covering insubordinate, missionary doctrine could make exposure sinful, and colonial public life could make older forms of Bengali dress socially inadmissible. The garments differed. The recurring demand was that women’s dress make obedience visible.

Today, the lesson arrives in ordinary words: orna thik koro (Fix your orna). Pull it forward. Do not let it slip. The girl is not only being taught how to arrange fabric. She is learning that her body can disrupt a room, that other people’s looking is a condition she must manage, and that respectability is something she carries on her shoulders. Soon she adjusts the cloth before anyone asks. Authority has completed its most efficient transformation: the command now feels like instinct.

Why is there so much anxiety about women’s bodies?

Covering and its many politics

This is not to say that every act of covering is oppressive. Cloth can be chosen, pleasurable, devotional, protective and defiant. Nadar women show why exposure is not a universal synonym for freedom; Pacific women show that wearers can transform an imposed garment. The orna, too, can be prayer, beauty, intimacy, fashion or refusal. Fabric never has only one political life. But women’s ability to remake cloth does not absolve the authorities that make it their responsibility. The female body remains where society stages its arguments about caste, civilisation, religion, sexuality and honour.

The deepest fiction of modesty is therefore not that one particular amount of covering is universally right. It is that the rule originates in the body being regulated—a body that does not ask to become a caste register, evidence of civilisation or a family’s moral boundary, until someone looks at it, assigns the cloth a meaning and calls obedience virtue.

By the time a girl reaches for her orna without thinking, the people who wrote the rule have vanished from the room. Their authority remains—in her hands, adjusting the fabric.

Syeda Shagufe Hossain is a feminist writer, gender justice practitioner and movement-builder. This is the first article in a series of eight exploring how faith, ritual and culture shape women’s bodies and lives.
